desc:
For a positive integer x, let s(x) be the sum of the squares of its decimal digits. For example s(47) = 42 + 72 = 65.

Given target, return the smallest positive integer x with s(x) = target. The answer can be very long, so return it as a string of decimal digits with no leading zeros.

target = 1   -> "1"
target = 5   -> "12"   (12 + 22 = 5)
target = 82  -> "19"   (12 + 92 = 82)
target = 81  -> "9"
hints: The order of the digits does not change the square sum, and the smallest number is the one with the fewest digits. Start by asking for the minimum number of digits.

Digits 0 never help, because they add a digit without changing the sum. Find the smallest length L such that target is a sum of exactly L squares of digits 1 to 9, then pick the digits from the left, always trying the smallest one first.

Let reach[r] be the set of sums that can be written with exactly r digits from 1 to 9, stored as a bitmask. A digit d extends a sum by d squared. At each position choose the smallest d for which the remaining sum is in reach for the digits still to place.
editorial: Zeros never help. A zero adds one digit without changing the square sum, so removing it gives a shorter number with the same sum. The answer therefore uses only digits 1 to 9. Its length L is the smallest r for which target is a sum of exactly r squares of nonzero digits, and every number of that length is smaller than any longer number.

Compute the sets reach[0], reach[1], ... as bitmasks: reach[0] contains only sum 0, and reach[r] is the union over d from 1 to 9 of reach[r-1] shifted left by d<sup>2</sup>, limited to sums up to target. Stop at the first r whose set contains target; that r is L.

Build the answer greedily from the left. With rem still to cover and L - p - 1 digits after position p, choose the smallest d such that d<sup>2</sup> is at most rem and rem - d<sup>2</sup> is in reach[L - p - 1]. This gives the lexicographically smallest string of length L, which is the smallest number of that length. The bit operations take about O(target<sup>2</sup> / 64) time.
